title: Arachnode — Automated Job Discovery & Outreach Platform
subtitle: Automated Job Discovery & Outreach Platform
story: Built because I genuinely needed it — manually tracking job postings and cold-emailing recruiters was unscalable as placement season approached.
bullets: Architected across 7 independent microservices communicating via Redis Streams consumer groups — chose Redis Streams over Kafka for at-least-once delivery with lower operational overhead for a self-hosted deployment.
4-tier test suite: unit, integration (testcontainers with ephemeral Postgres + Redis), contract (schema consistency across services), and e2e (full dashboard flows).
OSINT recruiter enrichment (GitHub API + SMTP verification) and Ollama-powered cold-email drafting via Jinja2; full pipeline automated via APScheduler.
Serves as Project Admin: reviewing PRs, enforcing API contracts, managing CI/GitHub Actions, mentoring GSSoC / ELUSOC contributors.
problem: Engineering placement season means manually checking Wellfound, Naukri, LinkedIn, and a dozen other platforms every day, copy-pasting cold emails, and losing track of every company you've reached out to — with no structure and no automation.
solution: Built a self-hosted microservice system that crawls startup job boards, scrapes structured platforms, discovers hiring manager contacts via OSINT, and drafts personalized cold emails using a locally running LLM — all automated on a schedule.
architecture: Scheduler → Crawler Service (Scrapy + Playwright) + Platform Scraper (Playwright + httpx) → Redis Streams → Aggregator (FastAPI + PostgreSQL) → Contact Discovery Service → Cold Email Generator (Jinja2 + Ollama) → API Gateway → Vanilla JS Dashboard
impact: 26 stars, 47 forks — serves as Project Admin reviewing PRs and mentoring GSSoC / ELUSOC contributors.
role: Designed the full microservice architecture, implemented the crawler and ATS detection pipeline, built the Redis Streams event backbone, developed the contact discovery OSINT pipeline, integrated Ollama for local LLM email generation, and authored the contributor infrastructure.

title: HPMS — Hostel Permission Management System
subtitle: Hostel Permission Management System
story: Hostel students had to hand-write permission letters on A4 sheets — wardens often unavailable, no audit trail. I designed the full digital replacement.
bullets: 5-role permission workflow (Student / Warden / Chief Warden / Admin / Security) with JWT-signed QR certificates generated on approval — valid for exactly 2 scans (exit + entry), auto-invalidated after both.

Modular monolith backend (Node.js + Express + Prisma) across 7 feature modules: auth, users, master, requests, certificates, gate, admin — served behind Nginx reverse proxy with SSL termination for HTTPS-required camera access at the gate.
Gate scanner web app using html5-qrcode; node-cron job detecting overdue returns and triggering warden alerts; SMTP notifications to parents on approval, exit, and return.

Attempted Tatvik TMF20 biometric integration: built a .NET 4.8 bridge exposing the SDK over HTTP and a .NET 8 FingerprintService calling it — hit a firmware wall (SDK couldn't talk to third parties); pivoted to the QR-based flow as the production solution.
Full SRS with 40+ FRs, ERD, and 4 system process flow diagrams; proposed to college administration for deployment.
problem: Hostel students had to hand-write permission letters on A4 sheets — wardens often unavailable, the process was slow and had no audit trail.
solution: Designed a full digital replacement: a 5-role permission workflow with JWT-signed QR certificates, automated overdue-return detection, and an Nginx reverse proxy backend.
architecture: Gate Scanner Web App (html5-qrcode) → Nginx Reverse Proxy → Node.js (Express + Prisma) → PostgreSQL
impact: Full SRS with 40+ functional requirements, ERD, and 4 system process flow diagrams — proposed to college administration.
role: Designed and implemented the backend architecture, database schema, authentication system, workflow APIs, and role-based authorization logic.

title: Appraisal Management System
subtitle: Faculty Workflow Backend
story: The college's faculty appraisal process was entirely paper-based — no audit trail, no consistency. I built the backend to replace it.
bullets: State-machine workflow: DRAFT → SUBMITTED → HOD_REVIEWED → FINALIZED → LOCKED, with legal revert paths and immutability post-finalization.
Full audit trail on every transition (userId, timestamp, old/new value); JWT auth with RBAC across Faculty / HOD / Principal / Admin roles.
Configurable scoring weights validated to sum to 100%; 13 Flyway migrations; @Valid on all endpoints; env-injected credentials via Docker Compose.
problem: The college's faculty appraisal process was entirely paper-based — no audit trail, no consistency.
solution: I built the backend to replace it: a state-machine workflow validating transitions from draft to locked status with role-based access control and full database migrations.
architecture: Spring Boot Monolith → Service & Validation Layer → Hibernate ORM → PostgreSQL
impact: Replaced manual appraisal handling with a structured workflow-driven platform, ensuring legal revert paths and immutability post-finalization.
role: Designed the state machine transitions, secured endpoints using Spring Security and JWT, wrote Flyway migrations, and implemented model validation.

title: Academic Timetable Scheduling Engine
subtitle: Constraint-Based Academic Scheduler
story: Departments spend days generating timetables manually each semester. The constraint-satisfaction problem hooked me.
bullets: Greedy constraint-propagation engine enforcing 8 hard constraints: no double-booking across faculty/room/section, 55-min consecutive-class gap, designation load caps, room-type matching, break isolation.
Section-first generation strategy prevents slot starvation; fallback faculty via priority-ranked FacultyPreference entries before failing.
Generates conflict-free timetables in under 2 minutes vs. days manually; H2 integration tests, Flyway V1–V10, Excel/PDF export, two-stage Docker build.
problem: University timetables were created manually — managing 40+ sections, hundreds of course assignments, room constraints, and faculty load limits with no automatic conflict detection.
solution: Built a constraint-based scheduling engine that automatically assigns courses to time slots and rooms while enforcing faculty load limits, room capacity rules, section conflicts, and institutional break windows.
architecture: React Admin Dashboard → Spring Boot REST API → Constraint Scheduling Engine → PostgreSQL (Flyway migrations)
impact: Generates conflict-free timetables in under 2 minutes vs. days of manual scheduling; H2 integration tests, Excel/PDF export.
role: Designed the domain model, implemented the scheduling algorithm, built the REST API, and developed the admin dashboard.

title: Offline AI Assistant Shell
subtitle: Sandboxed LLM in a C Shell
story: I wanted AI assistance in my terminal, locally, with no internet. Making it safe on a live system turned it into a real security engineering problem.
bullets: Sandboxed C shell integrating TinyLlama-1.1B via llama.cpp — fully offline, air-gapped execution post-setup.
Four-layer security: Seccomp syscall whitelist, PID/mount namespace isolation, capability dropping, rlimit caps — prevents privilege escalation and system exposure.
First-query latency ~2–3s (model load); subsequent ~1–2s; 10–20 tok/s CPU at ~1–1.5GB memory. Includes functional test suite, MD5 integrity check, and strace syscall audit workflow.
problem: Developers rely on online AI assistants, but integrating AI directly into system environments introduces major security risks such as privilege escalation, unsafe system calls, and data exposure.
solution: Built a custom C-based shell with an embedded offline LLM assistant using llama.cpp, designed with a security-first architecture including syscall filtering, namespace isolation, and resource limits.
architecture: Custom C Shell → Sandboxed AI Worker → llama.cpp Inference Engine → TinyLlama Local Model
impact: Enables private, offline AI assistance directly inside the terminal while enforcing strict syscall filtering and process isolation.
role: Designed the shell architecture, implemented sandboxed AI worker execution, integrated local LLM inference, and engineered syscall filtering with Seccomp.

title: MoodHarmonics — End-to-End AI Music Generation System
subtitle: End-to-End AI Music Generation System
story: Not another AI music app — the goal was to answer: can multiple ML models with different runtimes be orchestrated into a reliable, end-to-end system?
bullets: Orchestrated 3 heterogeneous ML models: MusicGen (text-to-audio), a fine-tuned GPT lyric model (enforcing verse/chorus structure vs. base GPT descriptive output), and YAMNet + GTZAN classifier (genre + confidence score) — all behind a single Flask API layer.
Model preloading at server startup + graceful fallback paths (local inference preferred, Hugging Face fallback) to manage heavy initialization and failure modes under real performance constraints.

Stored semi-structured song metadata and hashed user credentials in MongoDB; served generated audio from local file storage; coordinated frontend-backend interactions under CORS and latency constraints.
problem: AI media generation often requires multiple specialized models for text, audio, and classification. Coordinating these models while managing heavy inference workloads and reliability is a systems challenge.
solution: Built an end-to-end ML system that converts text prompts into generated music and lyrics while automatically classifying genre using audio embeddings.
architecture: React UI → Flask API → Model Orchestration Layer → (MusicGen | GPT-based Lyrics | YAMNet Classification) → MongoDB + Local Storage
impact: Built during Infosys Springboard internship — 45% latency reduction via preloading (2.2s → 1.2s avg initialization).
role: Designed the ML orchestration pipeline, implemented model preloading to reduce inference latency, and built API layers to expose AI capabilities to the frontend.

title: Air Notepad — Gesture-Based Drawing System
subtitle: Gesture-Based Drawing with Computer Vision
story: Built for fun — wanted my own air-drawing Paint app. The LinkedIn post reached 176,000+ impressions.
bullets: Tracked 21 hand landmarks per hand via MediaPipe Hand Landmarker, mapping raw landmark coordinates to drawing strokes via weighted moving-average smoothing (configurable factor) to reduce jitter.
Dual-hand control: left hand for tool/color selection via pinch gesture (Euclidean distance threshold); right hand for drawing via index-finger extension detection using relative Y-coordinates.
HD canvas (1280×720), 3 tools (Pen/Brush/Eraser), 8-color palette; confidence thresholds at 0.8 for both detection and tracking; frame-by-frame NumPy array operations for minimal latency.
problem: Traditional input devices limit natural human-computer interaction. This project explores how computer vision can convert hand movements into structured drawing commands in real time.
solution: Built a gesture-controlled drawing interface using MediaPipe hand landmark detection. Raw hand keypoints are processed with custom gesture recognition and smoothing algorithms to convert finger motion into stable drawing strokes.
architecture: Webcam → MediaPipe Hand Landmarks → Gesture Recognition → Coordinate Smoothing → OpenCV Canvas Rendering
impact: 176,000+ LinkedIn impressions — proof that something built from pure curiosity can resonate widely.
role: Designed gesture recognition logic, implemented smoothing algorithms to stabilize drawing strokes, and built the real-time computer vision processing pipeline.
